claims.text: Replacing an EAM thermodynamic-integration reference with a deep neural network potential trained on ab initio liquid and high-temperature solid configurations will improve reference–target phase-space overlap.
Improved phase-space overlap will reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch near the melting temperature.
The intervention applies to multicomponent, near-equimolar high-entropy alloys in liquid and coexisting solid phases near melting.
A deep neural network potential can be used to describe both solid and liquid states of a multicomponent high-entropy material and calculate melting behavior.
The proposed neural network reference should be trained on a wide set of ab initio liquid and pertinent solid configurations.
High-entropy alloys typically contain at least five principal metallic components in near-equimolar proportions.
The applicable temperature range is approximately 0.9 Tm to Tm.
Configurational diversity is highest between approximately 0.9 Tm and Tm.
A machine-learned potential captures the diverse local configurations of an ab initio liquid better than EAM.
The proposed machine-learned potential captures many-body interactions better than the pairwise or simple many-body approximations inherent in EAM.
Training on extensive ab initio data allows a deep neural network potential to reproduce complex many-body energy landscapes and nonlinear atomic interactions more accurately.
More accurate reproduction of the ab initio energy landscape bridges the gap between the reference and target potentials.
Bridging the reference–target energy-landscape gap leads to smoother free-energy integration.
The intervention will reduce thermodynamic-integration path-mismatch errors by roughly 30–50% relative to EAM references.
The intervention will improve free-energy convergence relative to conventional EAM-reference calculations.
TOR-TILD currently uses traditional EAM reference potentials.
Traditional EAM references inadequately represent the broad configurational ensemble of high-entropy alloy liquids.
The approach should be most effective for refractory, near-equimolar high-entropy alloys near melting and may be less effective at lower configurational disorder or far from melting.
Training-set scope and machine-learned-potential quality will influence the quantitative improvement.

Failure to obtain a statistically significant improvement, operationalized as less than approximately a 30% reduction in path mismatch or no improvement in free-energy convergence, will falsify the hypothesis.
